pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 9-10. Read (and write) Roman numerals to 1000 including M, and read years written in Roman numerals — MCMXCIX = 1999; MMXXIV = 2024 — applying the subtractive principle (IV=4, CM=900) at larger scales. Consolidates Roman-numeral fluency and the place-value contrast in a real, dated context.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Year 5): 'read Roman numerals to 1000 (M) and recognise years written in Roman numerals'.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): not a CCSS-M topic; enrichment/history of number in some curricula.
• Operational details — Extend the symbol set to D (500) and M (1000) and the subtractive pairs to CD (400), CM (900); read/convert both directions. Years are the motivating context (film credits, monuments, clock towers) and are tricky because they chain multiple subtractive groups (MCMXCIX). Continue to leverage the base-ten contrast: writing a year in Roman shows how much longer and calculation-hostile it is than our place-value system.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 9, emerging): reads numerals with D and M additively (MDC). Tier B (age 9-10, secure): converts years both directions incl. one subtractive group (MMXXIV). Tier C (age 10, extending): reads multi-subtractive years (MCMXCIX) and explains why the notation is cumbersome vs base-ten.
bestPractices: Extend symbols to D and M and subtractive pairs to CD/CM; convert both directions.
Use years as the motivating real context (monuments, film credits, clock faces).
Parse complex years group by group (M | CM | XC | IX) to manage chained subtractive pairs.
Keep the base-ten contrast alive — note how long/awkward big years are in Roman.
Target multi-subtractive errors (IC for 99 instead of XCIX) explicitly.
keyRepresentations: Real artefacts: dated monuments, film credits, clock towers
Place-value contrast chart (what Roman still lacks)
commonMisconceptions: Invalid subtractive forms at scale (IC/IM for 99/999 instead of XCIX/CMXCIX).
Reading chained subtractive groups additively (misreading MCMXCIX).
Confusing D and M values or omitting a group.
Pure-additive over-long strings (writing 900 as DCCCC not CM).
Thinking Roman numerals gained a zero/place value.

learn.summary: For ages 9-10: read and write Roman numerals to 1000 (adding D=500, M=1000 and the subtractive pairs CD=400, CM=900), and read/write years such as MCMXCIX=1999 and MMXXIV=2024. The core skill is parsing chained additive and subtractive groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and understanding why, in the allowed pairs, a smaller symbol before a larger one means subtract. Keep a running contrast with base-ten place value: a year written in Roman is usually longer (though not always, e.g. MM for 2000) and is always awkward to calculate with compared with the compact four-digit numeral.

activities.title: Build and decode years with a symbol-tile decoder
feedback: If the string is read as a straight running sum (so IV becomes 6, or MCMXCIX is totalled incorrectly), highlight that a smaller symbol BEFORE a larger one is subtracted (IV = 5 − 1) while after it is added (VI = 6); then regroup into pairs.
If a learner writes IC for 99 or IM for 999, state the convention: subtract only I from V/X, X from L/C, C from D/M, so 99 = XCIX and 999 = CMXCIX (not IC or IM).
If D and M values are confused or a group is omitted, re-show the symbol→value chart and recount groups left to right.
When grouping is correct, name each chunk aloud (one thousand, nine hundred, ninety, nine) to confirm the decomposition.
activities.rationale: Live grouping and two-way conversion make the chained subtractive rule concrete and give immediate correction on invalid forms. Optional interaction examples: colour-coding each group, a value readout that updates as tiles are placed, and a flag with the corrected form when an invalid subtractive pair is built — these illustrate the mechanism but are not required or proven more effective than other media.
sourceClaims: Parsing years by subtractive groups and maintaining the base-ten contrast supports Roman-numeral fluency and place-value appreciation.
learnerActions: Assemble a year from symbol tiles including D and M, or read a given year such as MCMXCIX.
Split the year into coloured groups (M | CM | XC | IX) and state each group's value (1000 + 900 + 90 + 9 = 1999).
Convert both directions: read a Roman year into Hindu-Arabic, and write a modern year (e.g. 2024 → MMXXIV) in Roman.
Try an illegal shortcut such as IC for 99, see it flagged, and correct it to XCIX.
activities.intendedInsight: A long, intimidating Roman year is really a chain of familiar subtractive/additive groups; each group reads independently, and only certain subtractive pairs are valid.

activities.title: Roman vs base-ten contrast panel
feedback: If a learner thinks Roman numerals have a hidden zero or place value, point out that value comes from the symbols and their order, not from column position, and that there is no zero symbol.
Reinforce by counting how many characters the Roman year needs versus four digits (most years need more, e.g. MCMXCIX has seven, though a few such as MM for 2000 need fewer).
activities.rationale: Keeping the base-ten contrast alive deepens place-value appreciation rather than treating Roman numerals as an isolated curiosity.
sourceClaims: Parsing years by subtractive groups and maintaining the base-ten contrast supports Roman-numeral fluency and place-value appreciation.
learnerActions: Type or write a modern year and place its Roman form beside the compact Hindu-Arabic numeral.
Compare the length and readability of the two, and note that Roman lacks a zero and place value.
Try to imagine adding or multiplying two years in Roman form to feel why it is awkward.
activities.intendedInsight: A place-value system with zero is far more compact and calculation-friendly than additive/subtractive Roman notation.

activities.title: Read dates off real artefacts (guided)
feedback: If a date is misread, return to group-by-group decomposition before giving the full value.
Prompt the learner to justify why their grouping is valid (which subtractive pairs are allowed).
activities.rationale: Authentic dated examples supply the motivating context named in the pedagogy (monuments, film credits, foundation stones; clock faces give hour readings rather than years) and support both reading and spoken explanation. A guide/dialogue format may add motivation and spoken reasoning; it complements rather than replaces written conversion practice.
learnerActions: Look at dated monuments, film credits, foundation stones, or date inscriptions on clock towers that use Roman numerals (a clock face itself shows hours 1–12 rather than a year, and often writes 4 as IIII).
Decode each date into a modern year, saying how you split it into groups.
A guide or partner can read a date aloud and ask you to convert it, or ask you to write today's date in Roman.
activities.intendedInsight: Roman year notation appears in the real world; the same grouping skill decodes authentic dates.

constraints: Restrict subtractive pairs to the valid conventions: I before V/X, X before L/C, C before D/M; reject over-applied subtraction such as IC or IM, and use IV (not IIII) for 4 in standard writing, while noting that many clock faces traditionally show IIII as an accepted variant.

A static annotated artefact (monument date, clock face) is a useful reference and reading task but does not by itself exercise writing/producing Roman numerals; pair it with construction or two-way conversion for the full objective.

Matching and multiple-choice checks consolidate and assess reading, but recognition-only responses do not elicit independent construction of a year; include tasks where the learner writes the Roman form themselves.
Keep genuinely dated examples (real years) rather than only abstract numerals so the 'recognise years' objective is met.
Interaction examples (colour grouping, live value readout, invalid-form flagging) are illustrative, not mandatory mechanisms, and their efficacy relative to other media is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The pedagogy lists 'DCCCC not CM' as a pure-additive error for 900; this is consistent with standard convention (CM is preferred). Arithmetic checks pass: M|CM|XC|IX = 1000+900+90+9 = 1999, 999 = CMXCIX, and MMXXIV = 2000+20+4 = 2024.

Two source claims (CCSS absence; NCETM pedagogy) are marked verified:false in the row; do not treat them as confirmed. The DfE Year 5 statement is marked verified:true in the legacy data but has not been re-checked here. The DfE claim supports the curriculum objective (reading Roman numerals and recognising years) but does not establish the grouping/two-way-conversion teaching method, so it was not retained as a sourceClaim on the method-focused activity; the NCETM claim directly supports the grouping/base-ten method, though neither establishes efficacy of any particular interaction or medium.

The legacy 'ideal/strong/possible/poor' fit rankings and the claim that decoding is 'best drilled on a bench' are catalog preferences, not established efficacy; softened and not asserted as necessity.
The 3D-interactive 'no spatial dimension / adds nothing' judgement was dropped as a catalog ranking rather than an objective pedagogical law.

probeDeeper: Read MCMXCIX and show how you split it into chunks.
assess.correctAnswer: IV = 4 because a smaller symbol placed before a larger one is subtracted (5 − 1). MCMXCIX = M(1000) + CM(900) + XC(90) + IX(9) = 1999, read as subtractive pairs.

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds all symbols regardless of order: reads IV as 6 (I + V) or MCMXCIX as a running sum
errorPatterns.nextMove: Show that a smaller symbol BEFORE a larger means subtract (IV = 5 − 1); after means add (VI = 6). Group MCMXCIX into subtractive pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child treats every symbol as additive and gets 6 for IV or a wrong total for 1999.

errorPatterns.pattern: Over-applies subtraction: writes 99 as IC or 4 as IIII inconsistently, ignoring the same-power rule
errorPatterns.nextMove: Give the convention: subtract only I from V/X, X from L/C, C from D/M; so 99 = XCIX, not IC. Practise valid vs invalid pairs.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child offers IC for 99 or is unsure why IIII is disallowed.

responseLevels.gap: Adds symbols regardless of order, so IV = 6 and 1999 is misread.
responseLevels.full: Explains and applies the subtractive principle within the same-power rule, reading and writing years to 1000 (MCMXCIX = 1999, 2024 = MMXXIV).
responseLevels.partial: Handles simple subtractive pairs (IV, IX) but stumbles on multi-pair years like MCMXCIX or over-applies subtraction.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Ask: 'Why is four written IV and not IIII? Now read MCMXCIX for me — and tell me how you split it up to work it out.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The subtractive principle is the conceptual hinge: a child who only adds symbols reads IV as 6 and cannot parse the CM/XC/IX pairs in 1999; a child who understands order-and-subtraction explains IV and decodes 1999 by grouping. The reason tier exposes whether they see position as meaning subtract.
